title: Batch Annealer + Admission Ejector + Tail Surge Attenuator for continuous batching
creator: Aisha Raman
description: Goal: reduce p99 tail latency caused by microburst admission variability while preserving p50 throughput and unit cost. We will implement a three-part runtime feature: (1) a 'batch annealer' process that continuously reshapes open batches using a temperature-driven annealing schedule to avoid brittle batch boundaries; (2) an 'admission ejector' policy that detects requests likely to cause tail spikes and proactively routes them to graceful fallbacks (model-variant or queued retry) instead of blocking main decode paths; (3) a 'tail surge attenuator' that applies tiny, randomized pacing to high-concurrency paths to decorrelate token emission and reduce quantile stacking. This work touches kernel selection because the annealer will probe kernel fit score for candidate batch shapes and prefer batch shapes that improve kernel utilization for attention-heavy sequences. It also includes attention-related optimizations: aligning KV-cache prefetch boundaries with annealed batch segmentation to avoid re-materializing KV slices during kernel transitions.
acceptance_criteria: p99 end-to-end latency for target workload reduced by >= 20% on staging compared to baseline under synthetic microburst traces
p50 throughput not degraded by more than 5% at steady-state for the same hardware profile
no increase in token unit cost > 3% across evaluation workloads (chat, long-form generation)
feature gated behind runtime toggle + per-tenant config and documented in Console rollout panel
automated integration tests validating annealer convergence and ejector decision boundaries
canary rollout plan documented and verified with a small set of internal tenants
updates: 2026-02-12: Ticket created. Initial design sketch and success metrics added. Assigned to Diego.

2026-02-18: Design review with runtime team — decided to use stochastic annealing (simulated annealing variant) rather than deterministic heuristics to handle multimodal request distributions. Trade-off: slightly higher planner CPU but much smoother batch boundary transitions.

2026-02-24: Prototype of batch annealer implemented in branch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/3682. Early microbench shows 12% reduction in synthetic p99 for short bursts (seq_len 128) on a V100 profile.

2026-02-27: Admission ejector policy thresholds tuned after replay experiments. We added a fast-path feature that routes low-cost deterministic completions to a tiny distilled variant to preserve main-path capacity.
2026-03-02: Tail surge attenuator implemented as a per-eviction-window jitter (0–6ms). Staging A/B shows improved p99 stability under correlated arrivals. Preparing canary config and runbook.
Pending: formal perf run on dedicated GPU fleet and production canary with three pilot tenants.
notes: Implementation choices: annealer operates in planner thread with budgeted CPU per-second; kernel-fit probe samples only on first N batch proposals to limit overhead. Attention prefetch alignment adds a lightweight map from token-window->KV-slice to avoid full KV rebuilds when batch shape changes. We will add tracing tags (annealer.temp, ejector.decision, attenuator.jitter_ms) to help diagnose regressions.
qa_plan: Unit tests for annealer convergence, integration test against local runtime harness with replayed production traces, staged A/B at 5% tenants for 48h with rolling rollback criteria (p99 > baseline + 5% or error-rate regression > 0.5%).
postmortem_criteria: If canary exceeds rollback thresholds or causes customer impact, generate incident and include timeline, allocator state dump, and kernel-fit traces. Add to retrospective if p99 reduction < 10% after three iterations.
